impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that patent claims covering methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's headache patents, which cover methods of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies. A jury had found willful infringement by Eli Lilly and no invalidity, but the district court overturned those findings. This decision is significant for the pharmaceutical industry as it concerns the scope of patent protection for biologic drug classes, particularly antibody-based therapies.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent protection for biologic drug innovators by affirming that patent claims directed to classes of antibodies can satisfy written-description and enablement requirements even when the specification discloses only one specific antibody, provided the prior art supports the broader claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Creates potential barriers for generic and biosimilar manufacturers seeking to enter markets covered by broad antibody patent claims, potentially extending exclusivity periods for biologics.

impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to methods for detecting anomalous program executions using emulators and models of function calls are directed to abstract ideas under step one of the Alice framework, and whether the district court erred in awarding damages based on foreign sales.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict for Columbia, holding that the asserted cybersecurity patent claims are abstract at Alice step one and require further proceedings on step two. The court also ruled the district court erred in allowing damages based on Norton's sales to customers outside the United States. This decision has major implications for software patent eligibility and extraterritorial patent damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides clarity for technology companies defending against broad software patent claims by reinforcing Alice step-one scrutiny and limiting extraterritorial patent damages, reducing exposure in infringement suits involving global software distribution.
impacts.negativeImplications: University and corporate patent holders with software-related patents face heightened invalidity risk under § 101, and patentees are further constrained from recovering damages based on foreign sales of accused products.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that has granted an exclusive license but retained the right to sue third parties for infringement retains sufficient exclusionary rights to establish Article III standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who grants an exclusive commercialization license but retains the right to sue for infringement possesses a sufficient exclusionary right to satisfy Article III's injury-in-fact requirement. This clarifies standing rules for patent owners who license commercialization rights while retaining enforcement rights.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring license agreements can retain enforcement rights and maintain standing to sue infringers, providing greater flexibility in monetizing patent portfolios while preserving litigation options.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face a broader set of potential plaintiffs, as both licensees and licensors with retained enforcement rights may independently bring infringement suits.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was legally sufficient evidence to support the jury's finding that the asserted trade secrets were protectable trade secrets under California law, and whether the jury's inventorship finding for patent invalidity was supported by the evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, finding insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying ideas were generally known. The court also reversed on patent invalidity, holding that contributions of generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions. However, the court affirmed liability on a trademark counterfeiting claim.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides important guidance for defendants in trade secret cases that information which is generally known in an industry cannot be claimed as a protectable trade secret, offering a strong defense for competitors.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners face a higher evidentiary bar to establish protectability, particularly when the claimed secrets relate to concepts that may be generally known, even if the specific combination or application is novel.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether genuine disputes of material fact precluded summary judgment on inequitable conduct and Walker Process antitrust fraud claims relating to Tenaris's failure to disclose prior art (CYMAX documents) during patent prosecution.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment on both inequitable conduct and Walker Process fraud claims, finding genuine disputes of material fact on both issues. The case involves allegations that Tenaris obtained patents on coiled tubing technology while concealing prior art documents it acquired when purchasing a competitor's assets. This ruling sends both the patent-unenforceability and antitrust claims back for trial.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of inequitable conduct have the benefit of the court's reaffirmation that summary judgment requires clear evidence of intent to deceive; similarly, patentees benefit from the high bar for Walker Process fraud.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that acquire competitors' assets and then obtain patents on similar technology face significant litigation risk if they fail to disclose acquired prior art during patent prosecution, with potential antitrust liability under Walker Process.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and rejection of a doctrine of equivalents theory, and whether the district court properly struck certain damages theories.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed-in-part summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multicore processor patent asserted against Intel, addressing the extraterritorial reach of U.S. patent law and doctrine of equivalents. The court also addressed the propriety of striking damages expert theories for inadequate disclosure in damages contentions. This case has significant implications for patent enforcement involving semiconductor technology with global manufacturing and sales.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting claims against products with global manufacturing chains benefit from the court's analysis of extraterritoriality limits, potentially expanding the scope of actionable infringement.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with global operations face continued uncertainty regarding the territorial boundaries of U.S. patent infringement liability for products manufactured or partially assembled abroad.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims relating to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit issued a mixed ruling, vacating summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain communication system patent claims while affirming eligibility for others, and affirming infringement and damages findings including the admissibility of the damages expert. The court distinguished between claims directed to abstract mathematical concepts and those reciting specific technological implementations in communication standards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides important guidance that patent claims reciting specific technological implementations in communication standards may survive § 101 challenges, supporting patentability of standards-essential technology.
impacts.negativeImplications: Consumer electronics manufacturers like LG face continued patent infringement liability for implementing industry communication standards, and the split eligibility ruling creates uncertainty for portfolio valuation.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony is admissible at summary judgment despite the witness's lack of personal knowledge, and whether source code constitutes hearsay for purposes of proving prior art under the on-sale bar of 35 U.S.C. § 102(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that 30(b)(6) testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the corporate representative lacks personal knowledge of the events, and that source code commands are not hearsay. The court rejected the argument that the on-sale bar should be limited to sales expressly disclosing the prior art device's functionality.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent cases can more effectively use corporate representative testimony and source code evidence to establish prior art, even when original personnel are unavailable.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face expanded evidentiary tools available to challengers seeking to invalidate patents under the on-sale bar, particularly in cases involving legacy technology where original engineers are no longer available to testify.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to a pH measured at a temperature standard in the field, and whether the patentee was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the finding of no infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents by Mylan's proposed generic drug, holding that the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' is measured at the field-standard temperature of 25°C. The court also upheld the bar on Actelion's doctrine of equivalents theory. This decision facilitates generic entry for Mylan's epoprostenol product.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies benefit from the court's application of standard measurement conditions to claim terms, facilitating design-around strategies and ANDA filings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Brand pharmaceutical companies with composition patents face risk that claim terms specifying measurable parameters will be interpreted according to field-standard conditions, potentially narrowing the scope of patent protection.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent that missed the deadline for a mandatory stay of a district court action under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) may obtain such a stay by dismissing and refiling the district court action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent may not circumvent the statutory deadline for seeking a mandatory stay of a parallel district court action by dismissing and refiling the action. This prevents gamesmanship in the coordination between ITC and district court patent proceedings, ensuring that parties cannot reset the statutory clock for mandatory stays.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners pursuing parallel ITC and district court proceedings benefit from certainty that respondents cannot manipulate jurisdictional timelines to delay district court adjudication of infringement claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the 30-day deadline for seeking a mandatory stay under § 1659(a) cannot cure the deficiency through tactical refiling, limiting their ability to coordinate defense strategies across parallel proceedings.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly determined that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement features violated Section 337 of the Tariff Act by infringing Masimo's patents on wearable blood oxygen measurement devices.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing and selling Apple Watch models incorporating blood oxygen functionality covered by Masimo's patents, upholding the limited exclusion order barring importation of the infringing watches. The court found no error in the domestic industry determination, validity rulings, or infringement findings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with valid patents on wearable health technology can effectively use ITC proceedings to obtain exclusion orders against major consumer electronics companies, providing powerful enforcement tools.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major consumer electronics companies face significant supply chain disruption risk when ITC exclusion orders are affirmed, potentially requiring product redesigns or feature removal to continue importation.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding a patent infringement damages expert report and granting summary judgment of no remedy based on the exclusion of all damages evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report and vacated the grant of summary judgment based on absence of a remedy in a patent infringement case against Microsoft's Azure platform. The court found the district court applied an overly rigid standard in excluding the damages expert, effectively denying the patentee any opportunity to prove damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent plaintiffs benefit from a more flexible standard for admissibility of damages expert reports, reducing the risk that technical deficiencies in expert methodology lead to case-dispositive exclusion.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending patent suits face greater difficulty in obtaining early dispositive rulings through Daubert challenges to damages experts, potentially increasing litigation costs.

impacts.caseName: National Veterans Legal Services Program v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users, including the propriety of attorneys' fees and incentive awards to class representatives.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the approval of a $125 million nationwide class action settlement resolving claims that the federal judiciary exceeded its statutory authority by using PACER fees to fund expenses unrelated to the PACER system. The court upheld the settlement, attorneys' fee awards, and incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives, rejecting objections from a pro se objector.
impacts.positiveImplications: The settlement provides full or substantial reimbursement to hundreds of thousands of PACER users, and the approval of incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives supports the viability of public-interest class actions.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a non-party to district court litigation may file an IPR petition on behalf of or in coordination with a time-barred party, and whether the Board's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination invalidating FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent, finding errors in the Board's analysis of dependent claims requiring a 'predetermined time delay' for restricting access to sensor information. The court also addressed the circumstances under which a non-party (Qualcomm) filed IPR petitions challenging patents asserted against another entity (Roambee) on the filing deadline.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from closer scrutiny of IPR petitions filed by parties with no direct stake in related litigation, and from the court's requirement that the Board provide adequate reasoning for obviousness determinations on dependent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies using IPR as a defense strategy face increased risk that petitions filed by coordinating non-parties may face additional procedural scrutiny, and the vacatur creates uncertainty for challengers relying on prior Board invalidation findings.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a court may correct inventorship under 35 U.S.C. § 256(b) when the omitted co-inventor cannot be located, and whether patents are invalid for failure to name all inventors when correction is unavailable.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that patents naming only some co-inventors are invalid when the omitted co-inventor cannot be located and therefore cannot be added through the § 256 correction process. The court upheld summary judgment of invalidity despite acknowledging Fortress's good-faith efforts to locate the missing Chinese co-inventor. This decision highlights the critical importance of properly documenting and maintaining contact with all contributors to patented inventions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers can assert inventorship defenses to invalidate patents where co-inventors were omitted, even if the omission was unintentional.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies collaborating with foreign manufacturers or contractors face significant risk that patents may be invalidated if foreign contributors to the invention cannot later be located for inventorship correction.
